Subject: RFI: eviction policy and slotting for Dedicated reservations

Hi RoHan,

Thanks for taking our RFP. One of the evaluation items Procurement flagged is how Redwood handles eviction/slotting when customers transition burst usage into a committed reservation. Specifically:

- If our traffic spikes and Redwood uses burst capacity, how do you ensure those burst instances are honored if we later convert to a committed pool?
- What eviction priority rules apply across GPU families (A100 vs H100 vs L4) when capacity pressure occurs?
- Can you share a sample SLA credit model if eviction causes tail-latency breaches for critical routes?

We attached a short template with our expected scenarios (we'll attach the template in a follow-up). Can you respond with a matrix mapping GPU family + slotting policy + expected time-to-restore? Also please include any lead times for resizing committed pools.

Goal: include this in our weighted criteria for CP-2027-RFP-41 by next Tuesday.

Thanks,

Hi Alicia —

Appreciate the clear ask. Below is a concise response and a proposed attachment bundle (matrix + scenarios + a short playbook) which I've attached for your team to review. High level first, then the matrix we used.

High-level behavior (summary):
- Burst capacity is treated as a soft expansion of the committed pool. When a customer converts sustained burst into a committed reservation within a 30-day window, we automatically prioritize their workload replication into the committed pool to preserve warm KV caches and batch affinity.
- Eviction priority is: (1) spare/ephemeral spot workloads, (2) non-critical background jobs (customer-defined tags), (3) lower-tier GPU families (L4), (4) higher-tier GPU families (A100/H100) but only if slot packing requires consolidation. We do not evict sessions mid-inference for in-flight tokens; we let in-flight requests complete before eviction.
- For mixed-GPU fleets, we prefer instance consolidation over cross-GPU migration to avoid quality regressions; migration only when latency budgets are threatened or on explicit routing policy.

Matrix (excerpt): GPU family | Typical slot granularity | Eviction window | Time-to-restore (target)
- H100 | 1k token-min slots | 5–10s quiesce + 45–90s restore | target 3–7 min for full cache warm
- A100 | 1.5k token-min slots | 3–8s quiesce + 30–60s restore | target 2–5 min
- L4 | 2k token-min slots | preempt immediate with 1–2s quiesce | target 1–3 min

SLA credit model (summary):
- If eviction causes a route's p99 latency to exceed the contracted target for >5% of minutes in a bill cycle, we apply a sliding credit: 10% monthly usage credit up to 50% depending on severity and repeat occurrences. We can codify stiffer credits for enterprise contracts (e.g., fixed-dollar credits for critical workloads).

Lead times and scaling:
- Increasing a committed pool by a single GPU family rack: typical lead time 24–72 hours (provisioning + warm-up).
- Cross-family capacity changes with quantization/compilation steps may require 3–5 business days for production-safe rollout (kernel selection + perf validation).

Attachments included: eviction-policy-matrix.xlsx (detailed rules), slotting-scenario-3.pdf (3 slotting scenarios), redwood-burst-to-commit-workplan.docx (proposed timeline).

Next steps we propose:
1) We can run a short 2-hour workshop with your infra and SRE leads to walk scenarios and test a prioritized route (we can simulate eviction at low scale).
2) If useful, we will produce a tailored SLA appendix with explicit numeric credit calculations for CP-2027-RFP-41.

Let us know preferred times for a workshop.

Best,

Hi Alicia — quick answers inline, and we've updated the attached workplan with a pricing appendix and a worked SLA example.

1) Replication/warm-up: minimal action required from your side — signal the conversion in the Console or via our API and we orchestrate the slot reservation + cache warm-up. We recommend you also flag the critical route tags so our routing keeps affinity. There is a 1–3% transient usage uplift during warm-up; we do not charge additional one-time fees for the warm-up itself for standard enterprise contracts — it counts toward usage until the committed pool is fully provisioned.

2) Worked SLA example: for a 50M-token-month route at current list rates the monthly baseline cost = $X (line item shown in attached appendix). If p99 breaches for >5% of minutes we apply a 10% usage credit; in the example that maps to approximately $Y credit per month (see appendix, table row #3). We can replace X/Y with your negotiated committed unit price once we have that figure.

3) Burst uplift recommendation: for a 2-month peak window we recommend reserving 10–15% of your steady-state as burst-dedicated lanes (i.e., 5–8 GPUs of the 50-GPU pool) and rely on on-demand burst for incremental spikes. That balance minimizes committed cost while preserving low tail-latency. If you prefer an aggressive no-on-demand posture we can model 25% uplift but that materially increases committed spend.

Action items: I've attached the updated redwood-burst-to-commit-workplan.docx (pricing appendix added) and the eviction-policy-matrix.xlsx shows per-GPU family restore times. Let's schedule the 2-hour workshop on Mon/Tue next week — rohan, can you take the lead on availability?
